lesson.title: Insertion Sort: Building Order One Card at a Time
lesson.summary: Insertion sort grows a sorted portion of the list one element at a time, inserting each new element into its correct position, much like sorting playing cards as you pick them up one by one.
lesson.body:
If you have ever sorted a hand of playing cards by picking up one card at a time and sliding it into its correct spot among the cards you are already holding, you have performed insertion sort. Like selection sort, it relies on traversing a list and comparing elements, but it grows the sorted portion in a different way: instead of hunting for the overall minimum on every pass, it takes the next unsorted element and shifts it backward through the sorted portion until it lands in the right place.

def insertion_sort(arr):
    for i in range(1, len(arr)):
        key = arr[i]
        j = i - 1
        while j >= 0 and arr[j] > key:
            arr[j + 1] = arr[j]
            j -= 1
        arr[j + 1] = key
    return arr

The variable key holds the element being inserted, and the while loop slides every sorted element that is greater than key one position to the right, opening up a gap. Once the loop stops, either because j has gone below index 0 or because arr[j] is no longer greater than key, that gap is exactly where key belongs.

Trace this on the same list used for selection sort, arr = [29, 10, 14, 37, 13], to see the difference in mechanics.

i = 1: key = 10. Compare to arr[0] = 29, which is greater, so shift 29 right: the list becomes [29, 29, 14, 37, 13] and j becomes -1. The loop stops because j < 0, so key is placed at index 0: [10, 29, 14, 37, 13].

i = 2: key = 14. Compare to arr[1] = 29, which is greater, so shift 29 right: [10, 29, 29, 37, 13], j becomes 0. Compare to arr[0] = 10, which is not greater than 14, so the loop stops. key is placed at index 1: [10, 14, 29, 37, 13].

i = 3: key = 37. Compare to arr[2] = 29, which is not greater than 37, so the loop never runs. key stays at index 3: [10, 14, 29, 37, 13] (unchanged).

i = 4: key = 13. Compare to arr[3] = 37, greater, shift: [10, 14, 29, 37, 37], j becomes 2. Compare to arr[2] = 29, greater, shift: [10, 14, 29, 29, 37], j becomes 1. Compare to arr[1] = 14, greater, shift: [10, 14, 14, 29, 37], j becomes 0. Compare to arr[0] = 10, not greater than 13, loop stops. key is placed at index 1: [10, 13, 14, 29, 37].

The final result, [10, 13, 14, 29, 37], matches what selection sort produced on the same input, which makes sense: both are correct sorting algorithms, they just take different paths to the same answer.

The key difference from selection sort shows up in how much work each algorithm does depending on the input. Selection sort always scans the entire remaining unsorted portion on every pass, regardless of order. Insertion sort, however, is adaptive: notice that when i = 3 above, the while loop did not run at all, because 37 was already greater than its neighbor. If a list is already sorted or nearly sorted, insertion sort's inner while loop barely runs, giving a best case of O(n). In the worst case, such as a list sorted in reverse order, every new element has to shift past every element already placed, giving O(n squared), the same worst case as selection sort.
